subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Coffee in a Warming World
description: A 60-second lesson on Coffee in a Warming World.

hook.text: The World Coffee Research group estimates that 60% of wild coffee species are now at risk of extinction.

buildup.text: Wild species hold genetic diversity for disease resistance and climate adaptation. Losing them is irreversible.

discovery.text: Seed banks in Ethiopia and Costa Rica are preserving wild coffee genetics for future breeding programs.

twist.text: It costs just $25 million per year to fund global coffee research—less than what Starbucks earns in a single day.

climax.text: The future of coffee depends on investment now—in genetics, farming practices, and climate adaptation.

punchline.text: Save the genes today to save the cup tomorrow. Time is running out.

quiz.question: What percentage of wild coffee species are at risk of extinction?

details.summary: As temperatures rise, coffee farming is migrating uphill and into new regions. Ethiopian highlands, long the cradle of arabica, face severe losses. Meanwhile, areas previously too cool for coffee may become viable. This geographic shift disrupts established farming communities.
details.whyItMatters: The geographic redistribution of coffee farming creates winners and losers among communities that have depended on coffee for generations.
takeaways: Coffee farming is shifting to higher altitudes as temperatures rise
Ethiopian arabica heartlands face the greatest losses
New regions may emerge as viable coffee-growing areas

faq.question: Which coffee-growing regions are most at risk?
faq.answer: Low-altitude growing areas in Brazil, Central America, and Vietnam face the greatest threat. Parts of Ethiopia and East Africa where wild coffee genetic diversity exists are also vulnerable. Higher-altitude regions in Colombia and Kenya will be affected later but are not immune.

faq.question: Could climate change make new regions suitable for coffee?
faq.answer: Potentially. Parts of China, Nepal, and higher-altitude areas of existing producing countries may become viable. However, establishing coffee-growing infrastructure, expertise, and soil conditions takes decades. New regions cannot easily replace what is lost.
